title: Handling problems in a team

lead.text: Yes. When a team hits a problem, Rahul's pattern is to make it visible and checkable, so the team decides on evidence rather than opinion, and then to fix the process so the problem doesn't come back.

points.label: He turns disagreements into explicit rules
points.text: In the Drug Interaction Agent, explicit consensus rules decide when keyword rules and the model disagree on severity. In the voice-agent project, a release gate blocks a release on recorded evidence: missing scenarios, failed safety results or a drop in quality.

points.label: He raises problems early, even uncomfortable ones
points.text: He hand-reviewed every auto-graded call and separated test-setup artifacts from real defects. When the strict gate failed because 3 of 15 scenarios had no recorded call, he reported it instead of shrinking the suite.

points.label: He owns and corrects his own mistakes
points.text: When a ClinIQ revenue figure turned out to be a scenario rather than a measurement, he replaced it with an explicit hypothetical model and documented the correction.

points.label: He works problems through with the people affected
points.text: At Citizen Health he reviews grounded outputs with clinical input and translates patient needs into specifications. At Athena he iterated with product and software engineers against a reviewer rubric.

points.label: He has kept a group of people moving
points.text: As Vice President of the Data Analytics Club at UMKC he led a 30+ member organization, ran workshops and mentored students.

takeaway.text: For your team: expect someone who brings facts to a disagreement, owns his mistakes and fixes the root cause. The portfolio documents technical problems rather than personal conflicts, so ask him for a specific story in the interview; the pattern above is what you should hear.

why: A team problem is usually a disagreement about what is true or what to do next. The evidence shows how Rahul handles exactly that: he makes the facts checkable with tests, gates and hand review, he reports problems even when they make his own work look worse, and he changes the process so the problem does not repeat. Those are the behaviors that resolve team problems, which is why these examples answer the question.

title: Problem solving

lead.text: He finds the root cause, fixes it, and then adds a check so the problem can't quietly return. Four examples, each with the fix in code:

points.label: A realtime audio bug
points.text: When callers interrupted the voice agent, the model's memory drifted from what the caller had actually heard. He cleared queued audio and truncated the model's conversation item to exactly what was played.

points.label: A misleading metric
points.text: In ClinIQ he recomputed dashboard metrics from saved confusion counts instead of rounded headline numbers, and replaced a revenue scenario that could be mistaken for a measurement.

points.label: An ML pipeline, debugged before spending GPU time
points.text: For the diffusion model he measured the frozen VAE's reconstruction ceiling and ran single-frame overfit tests to separate pipeline bugs from undertraining.

points.label: A benchmark that could mislead
points.text: Added an audit that refuses to compute runtime ratios unless paired run metadata exists, with its own tests.

takeaway.text: For your team: problems get root-caused, fixed and guarded by a test or a gate, so the same issue doesn't return in the next release.

why: Problem solving is visible in what happens after something breaks. In each example he identified the real cause rather than the symptom, fixed it in code, and added a test, audit or gate to prevent a repeat. The failure write-ups show how each problem was detected and diagnosed.
